questions.question: A commercial pilot holds an airplane multiengine land rating and a rotorcraft gyroplane rating, but has no single-engine land rating. Without receiving supervision from an authorized instructor, what is this pilot's eligibility to act as PIC of a light-sport airplane?
questions.correct_answer: The pilot is not qualified to act as PIC, because light-sport airplanes are single-engine aircraft and the pilot lacks a single-engine land class rating.
distractors: The pilot is qualified to act as PIC, because light-sport aircraft operating under sport pilot rules do not require any specific category or class ratings.
The pilot is qualified to act as PIC, because the multiengine land rating automatically covers all single-engine aircraft within the same category.
The pilot is qualified to act as PIC, because holding a commercial certificate with any airplane rating satisfies the class requirement for all light-sport aircraft.
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 17, pilots holding higher-level certificates may fly light-sport aircraft provided they possess the appropriate category and class rating. The handbook specifically uses this exact scenario as an example, stating that a commercial pilot rated in airplane multiengine land and rotorcraft gyroplane is not qualified to act as PIC of a light-sport airplane without supervision from an authorized instructor, because sport airplanes are single-engine. The pilot must hold a single-engine land rating to act as PIC of a light-sport airplane.

reference.text:
In addition to the LSA rules, the FAA created a new sport pilot certificate in 2004 that lowered the minimum training time
requirements, in comparison to other pilot certificates, for newly certificated pilots wishing to exercise privileges only in LSA
aircraft. Pilots who hold recreational, private, commercial, or airline transport pilot certificates may pilot light-sport airplanes
provided they possess the appropriate category/class rating and a U.S. driver's license or medical certificate that meets the
requirements for the aircraft displayed in the 14 CFR part 61, section 61.303 table. For example, a commercial pilot rated in airplane
multiengine land and rotorcraft gyroplane is qualified to fly a light-sport gyroplane as pilot in command (PIC) if also holding a
medical certificate or a U.S. driver’s license. However, that pilot is not qualified to act as PIC of a light-sport airplane (sport airplanes
are single-engine) without supervision from an authorized instructor. 17-3

questions.question: A private pilot whose most recent FAA medical certificate was denied plans to fly a light-sport aircraft (LSA). What must the pilot possess to serve as pilot in command?
distractors: A valid U.S. driver's license, since LSA operations do not require a medical certificate
A valid U.S. driver's license along with a logbook endorsement from a CFI
A valid state-issued photo ID and a statement of health from a personal physician
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 17, while pilots holding higher-level certificates may normally use a valid U.S. driver's license as evidence of medical eligibility to fly an LSA, this exception does not apply if the pilot's most recent medical certificate was denied, revoked, suspended, or withdrawn. In that case, a U.S. driver's license is not sufficient, and the pilot must hold a valid FAA medical certificate to operate an LSA. This rule prevents pilots who have had a medical deficiency identified by the FAA from bypassing the medical certification process via the driver's license alternative.

reference.text:
Pilots holding higher level certificates with the appropriate category and class ratings may fly LSAs as long as the pilot holds a valid
U.S. driver’s license as evidence of medical eligibility. However, if the pilot’s most recent medical certificate was denied, revoked,
suspended, or withdrawn, a U.S. driver’s license is not sufficient. The pilot would then need to hold a valid FAA medical certificate
to fly an LSA.

questions.question: When selecting a flight instructor for a transition into a light-sport airplane (LSA), how should a pilot evaluate their options between a flight instructor-A (CFI-A) and a flight instructor-S (CFI-S)?
questions.correct_answer: The pilot should prioritize verifiable LSA teaching experience, as a CFI-S with this experience may provide better instruction than a CFI-A with minimal LSA experience.
distractors: The pilot should always choose a CFI-A because their broader certificate privileges automatically make them more qualified to teach in an LSA than a CFI-S.
The pilot must choose a CFI-S because FAA regulations prohibit a CFI-A from providing instruction in light-sport airplanes.
The pilot should choose a CFI-S because, unlike a CFI-A, they are specifically authorized to provide instruction in non-LSA aircraft like a Cessna 150.
questions.explanation: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, a transitioning pilot should choose a flight instructor with verifiable experience in LSA instruction. While a CFI-A is legally allowed to instruct in both LSA and non-LSA aircraft, a CFI-S with specific LSA teaching experience might provide better instruction than a CFI-A who has minimal LSA teaching experience. Additionally, a CFI-S is limited to instructing only in LSAs and cannot teach in non-LSA aircraft like a Cessna 150.

reference.text:
The flight instructor is an important link in a successful LSA transition. A transitioning pilot should choose a flight instructor that has
verifiable experience in LSA instruction. The Sport Pilot rule allows for a Sport Pilot flight instructor certificate, the flight instructor-
S. 14 CFR part 61, section 61.413 limits a flight instructor-S to instruction in LSAs—a flight instructor-S cannot give instruction in a
non-LSA airplane (e.g., a Cessna 150). While FAA policy allows a flight instructor certificated as a flight instructor-A to give
instruction in both a light-sport airplane and a non-light-sport airplane, a flight instructor-S with teaching experience in LSA might
provide better instruction than a flight instructor-A who has minimal teaching experience in light-sport airplanes.

questions.question: A pilot transitioning to a light-sport airplane is advised to fully understand the engine controls, procedures, and limitations. What is the primary reason this is especially important compared to transitioning to most standard type-certificated aircraft?
questions.correct_answer: Most light-sport airplanes use non-FAA-certificated engines that may employ significantly different technologies and operating characteristics.
distractors: Most light-sport airplane engines operate at lower rpm than standard aircraft engines, requiring different power management techniques.
Most light-sport airplane engines are air-cooled and require the pilot to manage cooling differently than water-cooled certificated engines.
Most light-sport airplane engines are fuel-injected and require different starting procedures than carbureted certificated engines.
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 17, since most light-sport airplanes use non-FAA-certificated engines, a transitioning pilot should fully understand the engine controls, procedures, and limitations. The source text notes that engine technology varies significantly from conventional air-cooled to high-rpm/water-cooled designs, and that most LSA engines are water-cooled, 4-cycle, and carbureted with higher operating rpm. Each distractor is incorrect because it misstates a characteristic: LSA engines operate at higher (not lower) rpm, are mostly water-cooled (not air-cooled), and are mostly carbureted (not fuel-injected).

reference.text:
Engines
LSAs use a variety of engines that range from FAA-certificated to non-FAA-certificated. Engine technology varies significantly from
conventional air-cooled to high revolutions per minute (rpm)/water-cooled designs. [Figure 17-4] These different technologies
present a transitioning pilot new training opportunities and challenges. Since most light-sport airplanes use non-FAA-certificated
engines, a transitioning pilot should fully understand the engine controls, procedures, and limitations. In most light-sport airplanes,
engines are water-cooled, 4-cycle, and carbureted. These engines have much higher operating rpm and require a gear-box to reduce
propeller rpm to the proper range. Because of the higher engine operating rpm, vibration and noise signatures are quite different in
most light-sport airplanes when compared to most standard type certificated designs. 17-6

questions.question: A pilot of a light sport airplane notices pronounced sinking and lifting sensations while flying across a terrain boundary where the surface changes from water to a hard surface area. What is the primary cause of this effect?
questions.correct_answer: Differential heating from the varying terrain surfaces creates thermal air currents that affect lighter aircraft to a greater degree than heavier aircraft
distractors: Wind shear at the boundary between water and land disrupts the lighter airplane's flight path more than a heavier airplane's
Mechanical turbulence generated by the terrain change creates updrafts and downdrafts that impact lighter airplanes more severely
The temperature difference between surfaces creates density altitude changes that reduce the lighter airplane's climb performance
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 17, differential heating from varying terrain boundaries, such as grass or water to hard surfaces, can cause lighter weight airplanes to experience sinking and lifting to a greater degree than heavier airplanes. The effect is caused by thermal differences (differential heating) between surface types, not by wind shear, mechanical turbulence, or density altitude changes. The handbook specifically emphasizes that pilots of lighter weight aircraft should carefully manage this weather-related risk when crossing varying terrain boundaries.

reference.text:
Due to an LSA’s lighter weight, even greater distances from convective weather should be considered the norm. While low-level
winds that enter and exit a thunderstorm should be avoided by all airplanes, operations in the vicinity of convection should not be
attempted in lightweight airplanes. Since it is not always possible to fly in clear, calm air, pilots of lighter weight LSAs should
carefully manage all weather-related risks. For example, some consideration should be given to flight activity that crosses varying
terrain boundaries, such as grass or water to hard surfaces. Differential heating can cause lighter weight airplanes to experience
sinking and lifting to a greater degree than heavier airplanes. Careful planning, knowledge, experience, and an understanding of the
flying environment assists in mitigating weather-related risks.

questions.question: While transitioning to a Light Sport Aircraft (LSA) equipped with an Electronic Flight Instrument System (EFIS), a pilot learns the Primary Flight Display (PFD) has failed. What determines whether the critical flight information can be routed to the Multi-Function Display (MFD)?
questions.correct_answer: The presence of a reversionary mode, which is not available on all EFIS systems.
distractors: The pilot's ability to manually switch the display inputs using the audio panel.
The EFIS battery backup providing emergency power to both displays simultaneously.
An FAA requirement that all EFIS-equipped aircraft must have dual display redundancy.
questions.explanation: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, some EFIS systems have a 'reversionary' mode where information from one display, such as a failed PFD, can be routed to another display like the MFD. However, the AFH explicitly notes that not all LSA EFIS systems are equipped with an MFD or reversionary capability, making it critical for a transitioning pilot to understand the specific system and its limitations.

reference.text:
If the LSA is equipped with an EFIS, the manufacturer’s EFIS Pilot Guide should be available for reference. In addition, the airplane
POH likely has specific EFIS preflight procedures that should be completed. These checks are to verify that all internal tests are
passed, that no red “Xs” are displayed, and that appropriate annunciators are illuminated. Some systems have a “reversionary” mode
where the information from one display can be sent to another display. For example, should the Primary Flight Display (PFD) fail,
information can be routed to the Multi-Function Display (MFD). Not all LSA EFIS systems are equipped with a MFD or reversionary
capability, so it is important for a transitioning pilot to understand the system and its limitations.

questions.section: Chapter 17: Transition to Light Sport Airplanes (LSA)
questions.question: A pilot preparing to transition to a light-sport airplane (LSA) believes that because the aircraft is "simple-to-operate" and "easy-to-fly," formal training is unnecessary. Which statement accurately reflects FAA guidance on this topic?
questions.correct_answer: The terms "simple-to-operate" and "easy-to-fly" do not negate the need for proper and effective training.
distractors: Because LSAs are inherently easy to fly, pilots can safely self-instruct during the transition.
Formal training is only required if the LSA is equipped with complex avionics or retractable landing gear.
The FAA allows pilots to bypass transition training for LSAs if they already hold a private pilot certificate.
questions.explanation: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook (AFH) Chapter 17, while light-sport aircraft (LSA) have been defined as simple-to-operate and easy-to-fly, these characteristics do not negate the need for proper and effective training.

reference.text:
Introduction
The light-sport aircraft (LSA) concept broadens the access of flight to more people. LSA have been defined as a simple-to-operate,
easy-to-fly aircraft; however, “simple-to-operate” and “easy-to-fly” do not negate the need for proper and effective training. This
chapter introduces the light-sport category of airplanes and places emphasis on transition to a light-sport airplane.

questions.section: Chapter 17: Transition to Light Sport Airplanes (LSA)
questions.question: A pilot preparing to transition into a light-sport airplane (LSA) is evaluating potential instructors. One instructor holds a CFI certificate and has flown several different LSA models years ago, but not the specific make and model to be used for training. Another instructor has fewer total LSA hours but has flown the specific training airplane recently. According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, which instructor better meets the recommended criteria?
questions.correct_answer: The instructor with recent experience in the specific training airplane, because transition training should be guided by someone familiar with that particular aircraft
distractors: Either instructor is acceptable, since any CFI with light-sport airplane experience can provide transition training
The instructor with more total LSA hours, because broad experience across multiple LSA models is more valuable than familiarity with one aircraft
The instructor with a CFI certificate is sufficient regardless of recent experience, because the fundamental principles of instruction transfer across all aircraft types
questions.explanation: The Airplane Flying Handbook (Chapter 17) states that a pilot transitioning into a light-sport airplane should follow a systematic, structured training course under the guidance of a competent instructor with recent experience in the specific training airplane. The handbook emphasizes that even though LSA flight may appear simple to an experienced pilot, the transition should include the same methodical training approach as transitioning into any other airplane. The key requirement is recent experience in the specific training airplane, not just general LSA experience or a CFI certificate alone.

reference.text:
Even though light-sport airplane flight may appear simple to an experienced pilot, a transition to a light-sport airplane should include
the same methodical training approach as transitioning into any other airplane. A pilot seeking a transition into light-sport airplane
flying should follow a systematic, structured light-sport airplane training course under the guidance of a competent instructor with
recent experience in the specific training airplane.

questions.question: A student pilot is reviewing the light-sport aircraft classification and notices that one common aircraft category is notably absent from the six LSA categories established by the FAA in 2004. Which of the following is NOT one of the six LSA categories?
distractors: Weight-shift-control
Powered parachute
Glider
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 17, the FAA's 2004 rule created six light-sport aircraft categories: airplane, gyroplane, lighter-than-air, weight-shift-control, glider, and powered parachute. While gyroplane (a type of rotorcraft) is included as its own LSA category, the broader standard aircraft category of 'rotorcraft' is not one of the six LSA classifications. This distinction tests the understanding that LSA categories are specifically defined and do not simply mirror standard aircraft categories.

reference.text:
Several groups were instrumental in the development and success of the LSA concept. These included the Federal
Aviation Administration (FAA), Light Aircraft Manufacturers Association, American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM)
International, and countless individuals who promoted the concept since the early 1990s. In 2004, the FAA released a rule that
created a light-sport classification for airplane, gyroplane, lighter-than-air, weight-shift-control, glider, and powered parachute.
[Figure 17-1]

questions.question: Can an aircraft holding a standard airworthiness certificate, such as a Piper J-3, qualify as a Light Sport Aircraft (LSA)?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, if it continues to meet the 14 CFR part 1, section 1.1 definition of LSA.
distractors: No, the LSA category is limited exclusively to aircraft specifically manufactured for the LSA market.
Yes, but only if the owner voluntarily re-certificates the aircraft under the Experimental (E-LSA) designation.
No, any aircraft with a standard airworthiness certificate is permanently disqualified from LSA operations.
questions.explanation: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, the LSA category includes standard, special, and experimental designations. A standard airworthiness certificated aircraft, such as a Piper J-2 or J-3, may meet the 14 CFR part 1, section 1.1 definition of LSA. If a type certificated aircraft continues to meet this definition, it may be flown by a sport pilot with the appropriate endorsements.

reference.text:
The LSA category includes standard, special, and experimental designations. Some standard airworthiness certificated aircraft (i.e., a
Piper J-2 or J-3) may meet the Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulation (14 CFR) part 1, section 1 definition of LSA. Type
certificated aircraft that continue to meet the section 1.1 definition of LSA may be flown by a pilot who holds a sport pilot certificate
with the appropriate endorsement for the aircraft (14 CFR part 61, section 61.315(a)). The sport pilot certificate is discussed later in
this chapter. Aircraft that are specifically manufactured for the LSA market are included in either the Special (S-LSA) or
Experimental (E-LSA) designations. An approved S-LSA is manufactured in a ready-to-fly condition and an E-LSA is either a kit or
plans-built aircraft based on an approved S-LSA model.

questions.question: A pilot holding a sport pilot certificate with the appropriate endorsements wants to fly a type certificated Piper J-3 Cub. Under what condition may this pilot legally operate this aircraft?
questions.correct_answer: The aircraft must continue to meet the 14 CFR Part 1, section 1.1 definition of a light-sport aircraft.
distractors: The aircraft must be re-certificated under a Special Light-Sport Aircraft (S-LSA) designation before a sport pilot may operate it.
The aircraft must be re-certificated under an Experimental Light-Sport Aircraft (E-LSA) designation before a sport pilot may operate it.
A sport pilot may never operate a type certificated aircraft regardless of its weight or performance characteristics.
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 17, type certificated aircraft that continue to meet the 14 CFR Part 1, section 1.1 definition of LSA may be flown by a pilot holding a sport pilot certificate with the appropriate endorsement, per 14 CFR Part 61, section 61.315(a). The J-3 Cub is an example of a standard airworthiness certificated aircraft that may meet the LSA definition. It does not need to be re-certificated as S-LSA or E-LSA; those designations apply to aircraft specifically manufactured for the LSA market.

reference.text:
The LSA category includes standard, special, and experimental designations. Some standard airworthiness certificated aircraft (i.e., a
Piper J-2 or J-3) may meet the Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulation (14 CFR) part 1, section 1 definition of LSA. Type
certificated aircraft that continue to meet the section 1.1 definition of LSA may be flown by a pilot who holds a sport pilot certificate
with the appropriate endorsement for the aircraft (14 CFR part 61, section 61.315(a)). The sport pilot certificate is discussed later in
this chapter. Aircraft that are specifically manufactured for the LSA market are included in either the Special (S-LSA) or
Experimental (E-LSA) designations. An approved S-LSA is manufactured in a ready-to-fly condition and an E-LSA is either a kit or
plans-built aircraft based on an approved S-LSA model.

questions.question: A pilot is considering building an Experimental Light Sport Aircraft (E-LSA) from a kit. According to the FAA definition, what must be true about this aircraft's design lineage?
questions.correct_answer: It must be a kit or plans-built aircraft based on an approved S-LSA model
distractors: It must be a type-certificated aircraft that continues to meet the 14 CFR part 1 definition of a light sport aircraft
It must be manufactured in a ready-to-fly condition and meet consensus standards for the LSA market
It must be built from scratch using an original design that has never been previously certificated in any LSA category
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 17, an E-LSA is specifically defined as either a kit or plans-built aircraft based on an approved S-LSA model. This distinguishes it from an S-LSA, which is manufactured in a ready-to-fly condition, and from standard airworthiness certificated aircraft (like a Piper J-3) that simply happen to meet the part 1 definition of LSA. The E-LSA designation is not for original designs—it requires the aircraft to be based on an already-approved S-LSA model.

reference.text:
The LSA category includes standard, special, and experimental designations. Some standard airworthiness certificated aircraft (i.e., a
Piper J-2 or J-3) may meet the Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulation (14 CFR) part 1, section 1 definition of LSA. Type

questions.question: A pilot is researching the design and certification standards of a light sport aircraft. Since S-LSAs and E-LSAs are not type certificated by the FAA and do not need to meet 14 CFR part 23, what standards govern their design and manufacture?
questions.correct_answer: ASTM Committee F-37 Industry Consensus Standards
distractors: FAA standard airworthiness certification requirements
14 CFR part 91 general operating and flight rules
Manufacturer-defined specifications with no external oversight
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 17, S-LSAs and E-LSAs are not type certificated by the FAA and are not required to meet any airworthiness requirements of 14 CFR part 23. Instead, they are designed and manufactured in accordance with ASTM Committee F-37 Industry Consensus Standards, which were accepted by the FAA in 2005. These standards are intended to be less costly and less restrictive than part 23 certification requirements, giving manufacturers greater design latitude while still providing a structured framework — not unregulated manufacturer-defined specifications.

reference.text:
It is important to note that S-LSAs or E-LSAs are not type certificated by the FAA and are not required to meet any airworthiness
requirements of 14 CFR part 23. Instead, S-LSAs and E-LSAs are designed and manufactured in accordance with ASTM Committee
F-37 Industry Consensus Standards. Therefore, LSA designs are not subjected to the scrutiny, demands, and testing of FAA standard
airworthiness certification. Industry Consensus Standards are intended to be less costly and less restrictive than 14 CFR part 23
certification requirements and, as a result, LSA manufacturers have greater latitude with their designs. ASTM Industry Consensus
Standards were accepted by the FAA in 2005, which established FAA-accepted industry-developed standards for the design and
manufacture of aircraft for the first time. 17-2

questions.question: Unlike traditionally certified aircraft, S-LSAs and E-LSAs are not type certificated by the FAA under 14 CFR Part 23. Instead, what standards govern their design and manufacture?
questions.correct_answer: ASTM Committee F-37 Industry Consensus Standards
distractors: 14 CFR Part 23 airworthiness requirements
FAA standard airworthiness certification requirements
14 CFR Part 21 type certification procedures

Instead, they are designed and manufactured in accordance with ASTM Committee F-37 Industry Consensus Standards, which the FAA accepted in 2005. These standards are less costly and less restrictive than Part 23 certification, giving manufacturers greater design latitude while still ensuring safety through industry-developed consensus standards.

questions.question: Why do LSA manufacturers have greater latitude with their designs compared to manufacturers of aircraft certified under 14 CFR part 23?
questions.correct_answer: Industry Consensus Standards are intentionally less costly and less restrictive than part 23 certification requirements
distractors: LSAs are type certificated by the FAA under a streamlined process that skips most testing
LSAs are exempt from all FAA oversight and may be designed without any certification standards
ASTM Industry Consensus Standards require more rigorous testing than part 23, allowing innovative designs

Instead, they are designed and manufactured to ASTM Committee F-37 Industry Consensus Standards, which are intentionally less costly and less restrictive than part 23 certification. This reduced restrictiveness is what gives manufacturers greater design latitude. Distractor A is incorrect because LSAs are not FAA type certificated at all. Distractor B is wrong because LSAs must still meet ASTM standards accepted by the FAA. Distractor C is incorrect because ASTM standards are less restrictive, not more rigorous, than part 23.

questions.correct_answer: LSAs are designed and manufactured to ASTM Industry Consensus Standards, which are less costly and less restrictive than 14 CFR Part 23 certification requirements.
distractors: LSAs meet 14 CFR Part 23 requirements but with reduced testing and documentation demands due to their lower weight and speed limitations.
LSAs are self-certified by their manufacturers without adherence to any FAA-accepted industry standards or oversight.
LSAs are granted blanket exemptions from all FAA design and manufacturing regulations due to their limited performance and payload capabilities.

questions.question: Which of the following elements are established under aircraft consensus standards?
questions.correct_answer: Design and performance, required equipment, quality assurance, and production acceptance tests
distractors: Pilot certification minimums, medical certificate validity, and flight review intervals
Type certificate data sheets, airworthiness directives, and supplemental type certificates
Airspace classifications, weather minimums, and air traffic control procedures
questions.explanation: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook (AFH), aircraft consensus standards include specific requirements for an aircraft's design and performance, required equipment, quality assurance, and production acceptance tests. These standards focus on the aircraft's construction and safety rather than pilot certification, traditional type certification processes, or operational rules.

reference.text:
•   Design and performance
   •   Required equipment
   •   Quality assurance
   •   Production acceptance tests
   •   Aircraft operating instructions
   •   Maintenance and inspection procedures
   •   Identification and recording of major repairs and major alterations
   •   Continued airworthiness
   •   Manufacturer's assembly instructions (E-LSA aircraft)

questions.question: Aircraft consensus standards (CAS) establish requirements across several key areas. Which of the following best represents the types of requirements included in a consensus standard?
questions.correct_answer: Aircraft operating instructions, maintenance and inspection procedures, and continued airworthiness
distractors: Pilot certification minimums, medical certificate duration, and flight time limitations
Airworthiness directive issuance, service bulletin distribution, and type certificate data sheet preparation
Airport design specifications, airspace classification criteria, and ATC separation minimums
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 17, aircraft consensus standards include requirements for aircraft operating instructions, maintenance and inspection procedures, and continued airworthiness, among other items such as design and performance, required equipment, quality assurance, and production acceptance tests. The distractors are incorrect because they describe personnel certification requirements (A), FAA regulatory oversight documents (B), and infrastructure/ATC standards (C)—none of which fall under the scope of aircraft consensus standards.
